title: Handmade Incense Craft
summary: Dip the bamboo stick in water, coat it in incense powder, and roll it again and again — in that wrapping and rolling lies a mellow fragrance no machine can copy, and a craft passed down in Taiwan for a hundred years.
content:
Dip the bamboo stick in water, coat it in a layer of fine incense powder, and roll it again and again in the artisan's palm until the thickness is perfectly even — in that single act of wrapping and rolling lies a mellow fragrance no machine can ever copy. Taiwan's handmade incense craft has over a century of history, a traditional art bound tightly to religious belief and everyday life. From selecting materials to blending the scent, from rolling to drying, every step holds the artisan's experience and wisdom.

【The Incense-Making Process】
Traditional handmade incense passes through a long, intricate sequence of steps. First comes "material selection," using natural woods such as agarwood, sandalwood, Taiwan incense cedar (xiaonan), and cypress as the base, blended with medicinal herbs like gansong, clove, and cassia bark to compose a distinctive fragrance. Next is "mixing the powder," grinding the ingredients to a fine dust, blending them by a family recipe, and adding powdered nanmu bark as a natural binder. "Rolling the incense" tests skill the most: the artisan dips the bamboo stick in water, coats it evenly with powder, and rolls it repeatedly until it takes shape at a uniform thickness. Finally the formed sticks are arranged neatly on bamboo racks to "dry," air-drying naturally in a ventilated, shaded place for three to seven days — never in direct sunlight, which would drive off the fragrance or crack the sticks.

【Famous Production Areas and Incense Shops】
Taiwan's handmade incense is best known in Xingang, Lukang, and Dajia. Xingang in Chiayi, next to Fengtian Temple, is lined with incense shops — dozens of them century-old establishments — earning it the name "Hometown of Incense." Around Tianhou Temple in Lukang, too, gather many traditional incense shops, more than a few of them long-standing names run by the fourth or fifth generation. Each shop has its own secret formula, and their fragrances differ in character — some light and elegant, others deep and steady.

【Types of Temple Incense】
The incense used in temples comes in several kinds by function: the "standing stick" for daily worship is the most common, about one chi two to one chi six (roughly 36 to 48 cm) long; the "coil incense" for peace prayers can burn continuously for hours or even days; and the "lying incense" is often used for seated meditation. There are also incense towers, incense powder, and other forms, each with its own use.

【A Craft Under Threat, and Efforts to Preserve It】
As industrial incense-making has spread and environmental awareness has risen, traditional handmade incense faces severe challenges. The younger generation is mostly unwilling to take on this demanding craft, and with the soaring price of natural ingredients and tightening environmental regulations, many old incense shops have had no choice but to close. In recent years, the government and civic groups have worked actively to register incense-making as intangible cultural heritage; some shops have reinvented themselves as tourism factories or cultural-creative brands, opening hands-on classes where the public can make incense by hand, in the hope that through education and cultural tourism this precious traditional craft can carry on.

title: Temple Jiannian Art
summary: Smash colored porcelain bowls, snip the shards into dragon scales and robe folds, and paste them on one by one along the roof ridge — this is how the most dazzling skyline of a Taiwanese temple is pieced together from fragments.
content:
One glazed, colored porcelain bowl after another is smashed, snipped into the curve of a dragon's scale or the fold of a robe, and pasted piece by piece onto the temple's roof ridge — this is how the most dazzling skyline of a Taiwanese temple is pieced together from fragments. Jiannian (also called jianhua, "cut flowers") is the most sumptuous decorative art on Taiwanese temple ridges, fusing ceramics, sculpture, and architectural aesthetics to hang whole storytelling scenes high on the rooftop — one of the most recognizable features of Taiwan's religious architecture.

【The Craft】
Making jiannian is exceedingly involved: the artisan first shapes the basic skeleton of a figure or animal from wire and lime plaster, then takes colored bowl shards, glass, or ceramic fragments and, with special tools, cuts them into the needed shapes — the folds of a robe, the curve of a dragon's scale, the arc of a petal — and pastes them one by one onto the plaster body, finally adding details with paint, such as a figure's facial expression and the gesture of its hands. Throughout, the artisan needs both a sculptor's command of three-dimensional form and a painter's sense of color.

【Northern and Southern Styles】
Taiwanese jiannian has developed distinct northern and southern styles. The south (especially Tainan and Chiayi) is known for the "heavy and ornate," with full-bodied figures, intense colors, and dense composition — a single temple ridge may hold dozens of figural scenes. Northern jiannian leans toward the "spare and refined," with smaller figures, lighter tones, and more empty space. This mirrors the broader difference between northern and southern temple architecture.

【Master Artisans】
The most celebrated master in the history of Taiwanese jiannian is Ye Wang (Ye Linzhi, 1826-1887). A legendary artisan of the Chiayi region in the Qing Dynasty, renowned for his mastery of both koji pottery and jiannian, his works are preserved at Ciji Temple in Xuejia, Tainan and are hailed as national treasures. Later masters include Hong Kunfu (heir to the Quanzhou school of Fujian), Lin Zaihua, and Chen Sanhuo — the last designated by the Ministry of Culture as a "Living National Treasure" for jiannian, devoted to passing on the craft.

【Notable Works and Temples】
To see the art of jiannian, the best places include Ciji Temple in Xuejia, Tainan (works by Ye Wang), Jintang Temple in Jiali, Baoan Temple in Taipei (works by Hong Kunfu), and Chaotian Temple in Beigang. On the ridges of these temples, classic tales — the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, the Investiture of the Gods, the Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea — play out in vivid life.

In recent years, traditional bowl shards have grown ever harder to source, and some artisans have turned to fiberglass or plastic substitutes; this cuts costs but loses the texture and luster of the traditional materials. How to preserve the craft while holding on to the use of traditional materials is the most pressing question facing the art of jiannian today.

title: Temple Restoration
summary: "Repair the old as old" — not to make an old temple gleam like new, but to let its century-old timber, stone carvings, and paintings go on living in the very form they have always had.
content:
The hardest part of restoring a historic site is not making an old temple look brand-new — it is letting its century-old timber, stone carvings, and paintings go on living in the very form they have always had. That is the weight carried by four words: "repair the old as old." Historic-site restoration is a specialized craft that unites historical research, traditional artisan skill, and modern science, charged with bringing century-old temples back to their glory and carrying their cultural life forward. In Taiwan, as awareness of heritage preservation has grown, restoration has moved step by step from the early days of "renovate and rebuild" toward the professional path of "scientific restoration."

【Core Principles】
Taiwanese heritage restoration follows internationally accepted guidelines. "Repair the old as old" — preserve the building's original materials, techniques, and appearance as far as possible, without over-restoring or adding new elements at will. "Reversibility" — the materials and methods used in restoration must be removable or replaceable in future without damaging the original structure. "Minimal intervention" — disturb the original components as little as possible while ensuring safety. All restoration work must be thoroughly documented — in images, text, and technical notes — as a basis for future research and re-restoration.

【Notable Cases】
Taipei's Longshan Temple has been restored many times; its most recent major overhaul (2015-2020) invested hundreds of millions of NT dollars in a thorough renovation of the main hall's wooden framework, stone carvings, paintings, and caisson ceiling — a benchmark for Taiwanese heritage restoration. The restoration of Lukang Tianhou Temple focused on faithfully restoring its Hokkien architectural character, with the team even traveling to Fujian to study the architecture of the homeland. Tainan Confucius Temple, as the "First Academy of Taiwan," is treated with particular care in every restoration, always drawing intense public attention. Other important temples, such as Beigang Chaotian Temple and the Hsinchu City God Temple, have also undergone highly representative restoration projects.

【Challenges】
Heritage restoration faces no small number of difficulties. First is the "artisan gap" — the old masters of traditional wood carving, painting, jiannian, and other crafts are gradually passing away, while too few young successors follow. Second is the "difficulty of sourcing materials" — specific timbers, natural stone, mineral pigments, and other traditional building materials grow scarcer by the day. Third is the "balance between preservation and safety" — many old temples can no longer meet modern safety standards, and how to reinforce their structures without harming their historic character is the greatest test facing restoration teams.

【Laws and Policy】
Taiwan promulgated the Cultural Heritage Preservation Act in 1982 and has revised it many times, establishing a tiered protection system running from nationally designated sites down to county- and city-designated ones. The government maintains a Cultural Heritage Review Committee to vet the designation of sites and restoration plans, and in recent years has advanced a "restoration artisan certification system" to safeguard the quality of the work. The Bureau of Cultural Heritage under the Ministry of Culture oversees national restoration affairs, holding regular artisan training courses and restoration-technique symposiums, in the hope of cultivating a new generation of restoration talent so that the expertise and skill of heritage preservation may pass from one hand to the next.

title: Temple Architecture
summary: The two ends of the ridge sweep upward like a swallow's tail — the higher they rise and the deeper they curve, the loftier the temple's standing. Every line of a Taiwanese temple is a language of its own.
content:
Look up at a Taiwanese temple and you will see the two ends of the ridge sweep upward like a swallow's tail — this is the "swallowtail ridge." The higher it rises and the deeper it curves, the loftier the temple's standing. Every line of a Taiwanese temple is, in truth, a language of its own. Taiwanese temple architecture is the finest expression of traditional Chinese building art in an island setting: from the Hokkien style brought by Qing-era migrants from Zhangzhou and Quanzhou, to the Japanese elements absorbed during the colonial period, to the local Taiwanese character that developed after the war, it distills centuries of artisan wisdom and cultural depth.

【Basic Layout】
The basic layout of Taiwanese temples inherits the Hokkien building tradition of China, and falls mainly into:
● Single-hall type: the simplest layout, just one hall, common in small temples such as those of the Earth God.
● Two-hall type (two courts): a front hall (the sanchuan hall) plus the main hall, joined by a courtyard or covered passage.
● Three-hall type (three courts): front hall, main hall, and rear hall — the highest grade, seen in large temples such as Tainan Confucius Temple and Longshan Temple.
● With side wings (hulong): chambers extending from both sides of the main hall, usually serving as offices, storerooms, or subsidiary shrines.

Large temples such as Lukang Tianhou Temple and Beigang Chaotian Temple may even have layouts of five courts or more, grand and imposing.

【Rooftop Art — the Skyline of the Taiwanese Temple】
The most striking feature of a Taiwanese temple is its ornate roof. The main roof forms are:
● Swallowtail ridge: the two ends of the ridge sweep upward like a swallow's tail — the most recognizable mark of a Taiwanese temple. The higher and more curved, the loftier the temple's standing.
● Horseback ridge: a flat, straight ridge whose ends are shaped into one of the five-element forms (metal, wood, water, fire, earth), common in homes and small temples.
● Double-eaved hip-and-gable roof: the highest grade of roof, seen in official ritual buildings such as the Dacheng Hall of the Confucius Temple.

The ridge decorations are more remarkable still: the main ridge usually bears "twin dragons contending for a pearl" or "twin dragons guarding a pagoda" (the pagoda of the three star-gods of fortune, rank, and longevity), symbols of good fortune; while the ridge panels on either side carry jiannian or koji-pottery scenes from mythology — the Three Kingdoms, the Investiture of the Gods, the Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea — rendered in vivid life.

【Stone and Wood Carving】
● Dragon pillars: the coiled-dragon stone pillars before the main hall are the essence of a temple's stone carving, the dragon's scales, whiskers, and claws carved with extraordinary fineness. Early dragon pillars bore a single coiled dragon; later ones developed into the more elaborate twin-dragon, and even triple-dragon, forms.
● Stone lions: the stone lions before the temple gate come in pairs, the male (mouth open, paw on a ball) on the right and the female (mouth closed, guarding her cub) on the left, standing watch over the gate.
● Wood carving: the beams, brackets, decorative screens, and shrines inside the temple all carry exquisite wood carving, with common subjects of dragons and phoenixes, flowers and birds, and figures from stories.
● Caisson ceiling: the caisson (zaojing) of the main hall's ceiling is the most intricate wooden component, layer upon layer of brackets drawing inward to form a rising, spiraling dome — a craft of extreme complexity, regarded as the highest display of an artisan's skill, with Longshan Temple's caisson especially famous.

【Painting and Door Gods】
The beams and walls of the temple are covered with colorful paintings, mostly of auspicious motifs (dragon-and-phoenix harmony, blossoming wealth) or historical tales. The door gods are the most important paintings on the temple's main doors — different kinds of temples have different door gods: martial temples paint Qin Shubao and Yuchi Gong (military generals); Buddhist temples paint the Four Heavenly Kings or the guardian Weituo; Mazu temples paint palace maids or eunuchs. Door-god painting is regarded as high art, and Taiwan has produced many famous door-god painters over the generations, such as Pan Lishui and Chen Shouyi, whose works are treated as national-treasure-level cultural heritage.

【Northern and Southern Styles】
Taiwanese temple architecture shows a clear north-south divide: southern temples (especially in Tainan) are ornate, richly detailed, and intense in color; northern temples lean toward the plain and restrained, with more subdued tones. This owes to the different lineages of northern and southern artisans — the south is dominated by the Quanzhou and Zhangzhou schools, while the north is more deeply influenced by the Fuzhou school.

title: Koji Pottery
summary: From the same lump of clay, koji pottery is fired slowly at a low heat of only about 800°C — a temperature just right to draw a jewel-like luster from the glaze, rouge red and emerald blue, each piece a one-of-a-kind work shaped by an artisan's bare hands.
content:
From the same lump of clay that others fire at over a thousand degrees into porcelain, koji pottery is fired slowly at a low heat of only about 800°C — and it is precisely this just-right temperature that draws a jewel-like luster from the glaze, rouge red and emerald blue, brilliant yet never harsh. Koji pottery (Koji ware) is the most artistically valuable traditional craft in Taiwanese temple decoration. Originating in the Lingnan region of southern China, it developed a distinctive style after being carried to Taiwan by migrants from Fujian and Guangdong, and is hailed as "Taiwan's national-treasure art." Every piece is a one-of-a-kind work shaped by an artisan's bare hands, holding an irreplaceable place in the decorative architecture of Taiwanese temples.

【The Craft and the Beauty of Its Glaze】
Koji pottery is fired with low-temperature, multicolor glazes (about 800°C), utterly unlike high-fired porcelain (over 1,200°C). The low firing gives the glaze its distinctive "jewel-like" luster, colors vivid and bright yet not harsh — most characteristically "rouge red," "ruby green," "emerald blue," "amber yellow," and "bronze brown." Each artisan has a secretly handed-down glaze recipe, so every artisan's work carries its own personal palette. The subjects are drawn mostly from historical tales (the Three Kingdoms, the Investiture of the Gods), operatic figures (the Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea, Journey to the West), and auspicious motifs (dragon-and-phoenix harmony, the qilin bringing a son) — each hand-formed and impossible to reproduce with a mold, a one-of-a-kind creation.

【The Making Process】
Koji pottery passes through several intricate steps, every one a test of skill:
1. Shaping: modeling the figure or animal by hand from clay (specially chosen pottery clay). The artisan must master human proportion, the flow of drapery, and facial expression, working with only the hands and simple tools — an elaborate figure may take several days to shape.
2. Bisque firing: a first firing to set the form (about 700°C), hardening the clay body without fully vitrifying it, keeping enough absorbency for the glaze to follow.
3. Glazing: applying the various colored glazes to the bisque-fired body — the step that tests skill most. Different glazes take on different colors at different temperatures, and the artisan must foresee the fired result from experience, judging the thickness and pairing of the glazes with precision.
4. Glaze firing: a second firing to completion (about 800°C), in which the glaze melts and fuses with the body, emerging with a crystalline, translucent luster. Kiln temperature is critical — too high and the glaze runs and deforms, too low and the colors turn dull and lifeless.

【Master Artisans and Schools】
Koji pottery flourished most in the Chiayi region, known as the "Hometown of Koji Pottery." Among the masters over the generations:
● Ye Wang (Ye Linzhi, 1826-1887): the legendary artisan of Qing-era Chiayi, hailed as the "founding master of Taiwanese koji pottery." His works survive at Ciji Temple in Xuejia, Tainan, their figures vivid and their glazes deep and mellow, designated national-treasure-level relics.
● Hong Kunfu (1865-?): heir to the Quanzhou techniques of Fujian, his works spread across the temples of northern Taiwan, with the koji pottery at Taipei Baoan Temple the most famous.
● Lin Zaihua, Lü Shengnan, and other modern masters have continued to advance the craft and its innovation.
● Chiayi City is home to a "Koji Pottery Museum" that displays this precious cultural art and holds regular hands-on classes.

【What to Look For, and the Challenge of Preservation】
When visiting a temple, koji pottery is mostly set on the roof's shuiche du (the long decorative band beneath the eaves) and on wall panels. Look closely at the figures' expressions, the details of their costumes, and their dynamic poses, and you can feel the artisan's deft hand and invention. In recent years, with the high cost of handwork, too few young successors, and some temples switching to cheap industrial substitutes, traditional koji pottery faces a severe crisis of succession. Fortunately the government has placed koji-pottery craft under intangible cultural heritage protection and, through cultural-creative promotion, is helping more people come to know this precious art.

title: Temple Painting
summary: No matter where you stand, the door god's eyes seem to be looking right at you — this is called "making the gaze come alive," the hardest test a temple painter faces and the skill they are proudest of.
content:
Try taking a few steps left and right in front of a temple gate, and you will find the door god's eyes seem to follow you, looking right at you the whole time — this is called "making the gaze come alive," the hardest test a temple painter faces and the skill they are proudest of. Temple painting is the most vivid artistic expression in Taiwan's traditional temples, spanning door-god paintings, murals, and beam-and-purlin paintings; more than decoration, it carries rich religious meaning and folk tales. Every stroke of color, every composition, is a cultural cipher the artisan tells with a brush.

【Door-God Painting】
The door gods are the most representative paintings of a temple, and the first art a worshipper sees on stepping through the gate. Different kinds of temples pair different door gods:
● Martial temples: Qin Shubao and Yuchi Gong (military door gods), in full armor and bearing weapons, standing guard in awe-inspiring majesty.
● Mazu and civil temples: civil-official door gods (bestowing rank and emolument), in court robes and holding a ruyi scepter or peony, symbols of honor and wealth.
● Wangye and Tianhou temples: eunuch or palace-maid door gods, holding flower baskets, treasure vases, and other auspicious objects in elegant poses.
● Buddhist temples: the Four Heavenly Kings, or the guardians Weituo and Qielan.
A fine door-god painting depends on "making the gaze come alive" — from whatever angle you look, the door god's eyes seem to watch you, the supreme skill of the artisan. The god's face, the patterns of the costume, and the details of the armor all demand exceedingly fine brushwork to complete.

【Murals and Beams】
The paintings on temple walls and beams span an all-embracing range of subjects:
● Historical tales: the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (such as the Three Heroes Battling Lü Bu, or the Solo Ride of a Thousand Li), the Investiture of the Gods, the Generals of the Yang Family, and more.
● Religious themes: the Twenty-Four Exemplars of Filial Piety, the Eight Immortals Crossing the Sea, Guanyin delivering people from distress.
● Auspicious motifs: dragon-and-phoenix harmony, blossoming wealth, pine-and-crane longevity, magpies on plum branches.
● Antiquities compositions (bogu): still lifes of old objects (vases, scrolls, the zither and chessboard) symbolizing refinement and prosperity.
Each painting's placement follows rules: the dragon side (the left hand as one faces the deity) bears the dragon, the tiger side the tiger; the subjects on the main-hall walls must relate to the enshrined deity. Composition observes the principles of "honored above, humble below" and "honored left, humble right," with the important scenes placed at the visual center.

【Techniques and Pigments】
Traditional temple painting uses mineral pigments (such as azurite, malachite, cinnabar, and ochre), whose colors last and do not fade, still bright and lustrous after a hundred years. The main techniques are:
● Gold-rubbing painting (leijin): patterns drawn in gold powder over a black lacquer ground, glittering and magnificent, often used on the inner side of door panels or in shrine decoration.
● Flat coloring: laying multiple flat colors over a ground and then outlining the contours — the most common technique.
● Raised-paste gilding (lifen tiejin): building up raised lines in lime plaster and then applying gold leaf, giving the pattern a three-dimensional, relief-like effect.
Before painting, the wall or wood is primed (filled, sanded, and undercoated); then the design is drafted with a brush, colored layer by layer, and finished with outlining. A complete mural may take weeks or even months to paint.

【Master Artisans】
Taiwan has produced a steady line of master temple painters, forming a distinctive artisan lineage:
● Chen Yufeng (1900-1964): hailed as the "Painting Immortal," with representative works at temples such as the Kaiji Tianhou Temple in Tainan. His flowing, expansive brushwork and lifelike figures made him a grandmaster of modern Taiwanese temple painting.
● Pan Lishui (1914-1995): Chen Yufeng's outstanding disciple and a master painter of the old capital, with works throughout the major temples of Tainan; his door-god paintings are especially superb, and he was designated a preserver of important traditional art of the nation, his "living gaze" technique still spoken of with admiration today.
● Liu Jiazheng: a renowned contemporary temple painter, devoted to passing on and teaching traditional technique.
The works of these artisans are regarded as the highest achievement of Taiwanese temple art. Next time you visit a temple, look up and study the painted stories on the beams, and feel the cultural treasure these artisans have handed down through the brush.

【Preservation and Succession】
The greatest challenge for temple painting is "restoration" — old paintings weather and flake away over time, and restoring them requires an artisan of the same caliber as the original painter; otherwise the restoration can destroy the original's value instead. In recent years the Ministry of Culture has advanced a "traditional architectural painting restoration program" to cultivate a new generation of restorers, and has used digital photography to record precious originals, leaving a lasting record of this fading traditional art.

title: Temple Procession Performance Troupes (Zhentou Culture)
summary: Faces painted in five colors, ritual implements in hand, the Eight Generals clear the way for the gods with a solemn, measured tread — and these seemingly fearsome figures are in fact officials of the underworld's court of judgment, driving off evil and guarding the deity's passage.
content:
Faces painted in five colors, bodies in operatic costume, chains and instruments of torture in hand, the Eight Generals move slowly forward with an indescribably solemn tread — and these seemingly fearsome figures are in fact officials of the underworld's court of judgment, clearing the way for the gods, driving off evil, and guarding the deity's passage. Zhentou (literally "battle formations") are the most eye-catching folk performances in Taiwan's temple processions, fusing martial arts, theater, dance, and religious ritual. On a deity's birthday, a territorial patrol, or a major festival, troupes of every kind turn out in full force, clearing the way for the gods and guarding their passage with thunderous gongs and drums and consummate skill — the most visually striking element of Taiwan's religious culture.

【Origins and Functions】
The history of zhentou can be traced back to the ancient Chinese "Nuo theater" — performances that drove off evil by impersonating gods and demons. Brought to Taiwan, they merged with local belief to develop into a diverse and distinctive zhentou culture. In temple processions, zhentou serve to clear and purify the road ahead of the gods, drive off evil along the way, entertain both gods and people, and display local strength and community identity. Zhentou are also an important stage for temples to "compete" — whichever temple's troupe is the most elite and best-performing shows that temple's congregation to be the most devout and united.

【Major Types of Zhentou】
● Eight Generals (Bajiajiang) / Ten Generals (Shijiajiang): the most representative of Taiwanese zhentou. Performers paint their faces in five-colored patterns, wear operatic costume, and carry various ritual implements (chains, torture devices, fans, fire tallies), processing with a solemn, measured step. The Eight Generals represent the officials of the underworld's court of judgment — the Civil and Military Messengers, Generals Gan and Liu, General Fan (the Seventh Lord) and General Xie (the Eighth Lord), and the Great Gods of Spring and Autumn. The face painting is extremely exacting, each role's colors and patterns following fixed rules — the painting itself is an art form. Tainan is the birthplace of the Eight Generals, and each temple's troupe has its own distinctive style.
● Guan Jiang Shou (Chief of the Officials): originating at Dizang Temple in Xinzhuang, as famous as the Eight Generals but wholly different in style. A performance usually features three people — the Two Generals of Increase and Decrease (variants of Ox-Head and Horse-Face) led by a commanding chief. The movements are fierce and forceful, the footwork rapid and full of martial flair; with fearsome faces and tridents or ghost-head blades in hand, they cut an imposing presence.
● Song Jiang Battle Array: drawn from the tale of the 108 heroes of Water Margin, the most popular martial-arts zhentou in southern Taiwan. Participants wield an array of weapons (swords, spears, staffs, shields, rakes), forming battle formations and drilling attack and defense through martial routines. The Song Jiang Array unites martial training, community defense, and religious escort, with rigorous training and members drawn mostly from local youth. The Song Jiang Array performance at the Xigang Pilgrimage in Tainan has been listed as a National Important Folk Custom.
● Lion and Dragon Dances: the most festive zhentou in temple processions. Taiwan's lion dance blends the Hokkien lion (smaller and more nimble) with the Cantonese lion (more ornate and powerful). A dragon array usually takes over ten people working in concert, sending the long dragon tumbling and weaving through the air to symbolize the arrival of auspicious blessing.
● Electronic-Music Third Prince (Dianyin San Taizi): a uniquely Taiwanese modern zhentou that pairs the traditional Third Prince (Nezha) deity puppet with electronic dance music and neon lights. Performers don oversized deity headpieces adorned with LED lights and dance energetically to the electronic beat. Though this innovation has stirred debate between tradition and modernity, it has successfully drawn in the younger generation and become a dazzling calling card in Taiwan's cultural diplomacy, representing Taiwan at many international occasions.
● Art Pavilion Floats (Yige): exquisite "mobile stages," with elaborate scenery built on parade floats and live performers (often children) portraying historical or mythological characters, tossing candy to interact with spectators along the route. Tainan's art-pavilion tradition is the most developed, while the art-pavilion parade of Beigang Chaotian Temple is famous throughout Taiwan.

【Training and Taboos】
Joining a zhentou requires a rigorous training period. During practice, Eight Generals members must "close the hall" — no alcohol, no entering unclean places (such as hospitals or homes in mourning), and no eating beef (because of the divine generals' connection to the Ox Lord); once their faces are painted, they must not speak casually or eat before removing their makeup. The purpose of these taboos is to unite the performers spiritually with the divine generals they portray and to avoid profaning the deities.

【Succession and Challenges】
The greatest challenge facing zhentou culture is public perception. In the past, some zhentou groups became entangled with gang forces, leaving the public with a prejudice against them. In recent years many temples and cultural organizations have worked hard to overturn this image, bringing zhentou into schools (through university clubs and high school and vocational programs) and cultivating properly trained successors. The documentary film "Din Tao: Leader of the Parade" (2012) brought the issue to the big screen, helping more people see the sweat, discipline, and cultural depth behind the zhentou tradition.
